tech:architecture.title: Seeing Markdown CMS in Diagrams
tech:architecture.subtitle: The shared core, and the flows of the OSS and Commercial editions
tech:architecture.summary: This article explains how Markdown CMS is put together behind the scenes, using architecture diagrams. The shared core is this: the site folder is the source of truth, the build generates article JSON (the shared data.json format), and the display side only reads it. The OSS edition (GitHub edition) generates with Actions and is served by Pages, while the Commercial edition (Cloudflare edition, R2 update model) is saved from an admin screen to R2, and a Worker generates and serves it when notified through Queues. In both editions, no program runs on the display side.

tech:architecture.markdown:
I have drawn a diagram of how Markdown CMS is put together behind the scenes.
This article uses that diagram as its main subject, and explains the system in order.
There are two editions, but the core idea is shared.

## Three design principles

The starting question is: does a program need to run every time a page is viewed?
For a website that is updated about as often as a homepage, querying a database and assembling a page on every access is more than necessary.
So the design was narrowed down to three principles.

1. **Files are the truth**: Articles are not stored in a database. An article is Markdown, an image is a file, kept just as they are — directly readable by people, portable, and easy to back up
2. **Pre-generation**: Generation is finished before publication. What is distributed is only the generated result, as JSON or HTML
3. **Browser assembly**: The server only distributes. The reader's browser assembles the lists and the article pages

![Slide "Three design principles": files are the truth, pre-generation, and browser assembly](tech/architecture-principles.webp)

## The shared core is the "site folder"

The source of truth is a collection of Markdown files.
An article is written as Markdown with information such as its title and date (frontmatter), and placed in a "site folder" together with its images and the site settings.
The build reads that folder and assembles the article JSON.
The display side only reads that JSON.
Because the article JSON follows the shared data.json format, articles from several sites can also be gathered into a single portal.
My group of sites, including this blog, runs in exactly this form.

## The flow of the OSS edition (GitHub edition)

The OSS edition runs on GitHub's infrastructure.
You write an article locally in an editor such as VS Code, and push it to a GitHub repository.
GitHub Actions then runs build.py, performs the generation and the tests, and commits the generated output.
GitHub Pages serves the site, and the browser reads the JSON and displays it.

![Diagram of the OSS edition of Markdown CMS: five stages — Edit (User Terminal), Store (GitHub Repo), Generate (GitHub Actions), Distribute (GitHub Pages), Display (User Browser)](tech/architecture-oss-gemini.webp)

Generation runs only when you push.
No program keeps running on the serving side.
The OSS edition is released under the MIT License, with its [repository](https://github.com/oosawak/markdown-cms-oss) and [sample site](https://oosawak.github.io/markdown-cms-oss/) published.

## The flow of the Commercial edition (Cloudflare edition)

The Commercial edition runs on Cloudflare.
Its central form is what I call the "R2 update model".
When an article is edited in the authenticated admin screen, the article and its images are saved to R2.
The update is notified through Queues, and a Worker converts the Markdown into JSON.
If generation fails, the last successful version continues to be served as it is.
Distribution is also handled by the Worker, which delivers the pre-generated version from R2.

![Diagram of the Cloudflare edition of Markdown CMS: five stages — Edit (Admin UI), Store (Cloudflare R2), Generate (Cloudflare Workers), Distribute (Cloudflare Edge), Display (User Browser)](tech/architecture-cloudflare-gemini.webp)

The Dynamic Head/OGP Injection shown in the "Distribute" box of the diagram — the mechanism that injects per-page head and OGP tags — is being implemented as an SEO measure.

GitHub is not used to update articles.
However, the Commercial edition also keeps a GitHub-based update mechanism.
Articles and images are placed in a private repository, and on push, Cloudflare Pages builds and publishes them.
It is a separate destination from the R2 update model, and articles of the two models are managed separately.

## Placing them side by side

| Process | OSS edition (GitHub edition) | Commercial edition (Cloudflare edition, R2 update model) |
|---|---|---|
| Storage | GitHub repository | R2 |
| Where generation runs | GitHub Actions (build.py) | Worker |
| Distribution | GitHub Pages | Worker |
| How to update | Write in an editor and push | Edit in the admin screen |

What differs is where the parts live.
The core — "the site folder is the source of truth, and the display side reads the generated JSON" — is the same in both editions.
Even if the distribution source changes, the display side is built the same way in both editions, so the reader's experience does not change.

![Slide "The reading experience does not change when the infrastructure changes": app.js in the browser reads data.json and assembles lists and articles](tech/architecture-display.webp)

As a guide to which edition to choose, it looks like this.

![Slide "Which should you choose? — a reading guide": a flowchart for choosing an edition depending on whether you are comfortable using GitHub, whether you want to grasp everything yourself, and whether you need operational support](tech/architecture-guide.webp)

## No program runs on the display side

The most important part of this architecture is at the end.
In both editions, no program runs on the side that displays a page.
A program runs only when an article is updated and generated.
That is what keeps both the display speed and the smallness of what needs to be protected.
The thinking in [Keeping the surface to protect small: how Markdown CMS approaches security](https://oosawak.github.io/tech/#/en/post/tech/static-cms-security) comes from this architecture.

The differences between the editions, and how they are offered, are summarized in [The OSS and Commercial editions of Markdown CMS](https://oosawak.github.io/tech/#/en/post/tech/markdown-cms-editions).
